title: Achieving Compliance as a Platform Engineering Team by Helping Developers
gist: Davide De Paolis, speaking at Dev Summit Munich and interviewed by InfoQ, describes how a newly formed platform team degraded developer experience by pushing forced workflows and stale documentation, and recovered by shrinking the required AWS tag set, encoding rules as Service Control Policies and Tag Policies, and rolling out compliance in a prevent-detect-notify sequence. The reusable pattern is inform first, softly enforce next, hard-enforce only last — plus a Tour of Duty rotation between platform and product teams to spread context.

themes.theme: How a new platform team destroyed its own developer experience

insights.claim: A platform team assembled from experienced product-team developers with strong DevOps and cloud backgrounds still degraded developer experience, because it launched an ambitious roadmap (service catalog, internal developer platform, cloud centre of excellence) via forced workflows rather than adoption.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Staffing a platform team with strong engineers is not the risk control — rollout mechanics are; DX metrics should be tracked from a platform team's first sprint, not its second year.
insights.quote: developer experience declined. Success came from simplifying governance, prioritizing what mattered, and rolling out compliance incrementally through prevention, detection, and communication

insights.claim: The specific friction from platform migration was concrete and mundane: developers moved from one AWS account with broad, loose permissions to multiple AWS accounts requiring context switching, configuration updates, and new skills.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Multi-account AWS landing zones impose a real per-developer productivity tax that must be budgeted for, not assumed away, in cloud governance business cases.
insights.quote: They were used to having one account, and permissions were broader and looser. Now they had to switch contexts, update configurations, and learn new skills.

insights.claim: De Paolis identifies a recurring failure mode in which security and platform teams adopt a patronising, directive posture toward developers, and argues forced adoption rarely works while alignment around a shared purpose does.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Governance programmes fail on posture more than on tooling — a diligence question for any org selling or buying internal platform products.
insights.quote: Nobody likes to be patronised and told what to do,
insights.locator: 'At the same time, documentation was often lengthy'

insights.claim: Lengthy, outdated and hard-to-navigate documentation was a direct driver of the platform team's support load, producing frequent developer requests and voiced frustration about declining developer experience.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Support-ticket volume against a platform is a leading indicator of documentation debt, not of developer incompetence — instrument it accordingly.
insights.locator: 'At the same time, documentation was often lengthy, outdated'

themes.theme: Tagging: the second attempt that worked

insights.claim: An earlier resource-tagging initiative at the organisation failed outright, leaving ownership, cost attribution and governance inconsistent and largely manual — a concrete cost of treating tagging as a metadata exercise.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Failed tagging programmes leave organisations unable to attribute cloud spend at all — a hidden blocker behind FinOps and showback initiatives that look stalled for other reasons.

insights.claim: The restart of the tagging effort began by reducing the number of required tags rather than by adding enforcement, then standardized them using AWS Tag Policies and Service Control Policies to validate inputs and block creation of untagged resources.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Simplify-then-enforce is the operative sequence; a governance programme adding controls before cutting requirements is likely repeating the failure.
insights.quote: They reduced the number of required tags and standardized them using AWS Tag Policies and Service Control Policies to validate inputs and prevent the creation of untagged resources.
insights.locator: 'De Paolis’ team restarted the effort with a different approach: simplify first'

insights.claim: The team paired preventive controls with the AWS Security Hub Resource Tagging Standard to detect resources already out of compliance, so the rollout covered both new and pre-existing inventory rather than only new resources.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Prevention-only controls silently exempt the existing estate, which is usually where the compliance gap actually lives.
insights.locator: 'In parallel, they used the AWS Security Hub Resource Tagging Standard'

insights.claim: De Paolis states that tagging only succeeds when it is explicitly tied to outcomes developers already care about — cost visibility, ownership and accountability — and that framing it as 'just metadata' with defined rules did not work.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Adoption of any internal standard tracks whether it returns something to the adopter — the test to apply before funding a governance rollout.
insights.quote: Tagging only succeeds when it’s clearly tied to outcomes developers care about—cost visibility, ownership, and accountability.
insights.locator: InfoQ Q&A — 'What was your approach for rolling out tagging'

insights.claim: The successful tagging rollout made the required tags easy to apply via infrastructure-as-code and platform defaults, and led with visibility — showing teams what was missing and why — before introducing stronger policy guardrails.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Defaults in IaC templates do more for compliance rates than policy enforcement does, and cost less political capital.
insights.quote: We started with a minimal, opinionated set of required tags and made them easy to apply via infrastructure-as-code and platform defaults.

themes.theme: Prevent-detect-notify as a reusable compliance sequence

insights.claim: De Paolis prescribes a three-stage enforcement ramp — inform first, softly enforce next, only then move to stricter enforcement — and reports it proved reusable across other internal compliance initiatives beyond tagging.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A transferable rollout template for any internal control programme; its reuse across initiatives is the evidence that it is a pattern rather than a one-off.
insights.quote: Inform first, softly enforce next, and only then move to stricter enforcement. This is an approach that proved reusable across other internal compliance initiatives.

insights.claim: De Paolis frames technical policy as guardrails rather than handcuffs, with the explicit design goal of making the compliant path the easiest one, encoded directly into the platform via AWS-native tools including Service Control Policies, AWS Config, Security Hub and tagging policies.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Compliance encoded in platform defaults scales without headcount; compliance enforced by review does not — a margin question for any regulated engineering org.
insights.quote: We treat policies as guardrails, not handcuffs. The goal is to make the compliant path the easiest one.
insights.locator: InfoQ Q&A — 'How do you use tech policies'

insights.claim: De Paolis argues policies alone do not create compliance — how they are introduced matters — and prefers automated detection with gradual enforcement over sudden hard blocks.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Hard blocks generate workarounds and shadow infrastructure; gradual enforcement is the cheaper route to the same control coverage.
insights.quote: Whenever possible, we rely on automated detection and gradual enforcement rather than sudden hard blocks.

themes.theme: Focus, context, and the platform-vs-product dynamic

insights.claim: De Paolis prescribes defining a minimum viable governance model, prioritising by business impact, and explicitly warns against ignoring findings that are important but not yet urgent because they will become a crisis later.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A triage rule for security backlogs measured in thousands of findings — the important-but-not-urgent bucket is where future incidents are being incubated.
insights.quote: If you have thousands of security findings, you need to start somewhere. Focus on what’s important and urgent, but don’t ignore what’s important and not yet urgent, or it will become a crisis later.

insights.claim: Adoption improved once teams understood that compliance initiatives were tied to company success and customer trust, to the point that product teams incorporated the initiatives into their own roadmaps.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: The measurable success signal for a governance programme is whether product teams voluntarily put it on their own roadmap — a cheap adoption KPI.

insights.claim: For larger initiatives the team runs a Tour of Duty model in which engineers temporarily join the platform team or vice versa, generating hands-on feedback and pushing platform context back into product teams.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost organisational mechanism for closing the platform-product gap — transferable to any org where an internal platform is under-adopted.
insights.quote: For larger initiatives, we use a *Tour of Duty* model, where engineers temporarily join the platform team (or vice versa).
insights.locator: InfoQ Q&A — 'How do you communicate changes'

insights.claim: De Paolis treats communication as part of the platform product itself — explaining context and impact before implementation, using RFCs, internal documentation and live Q&A sessions — which he credits with moving the organisation from a platform-vs-product dynamic to shared ownership.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Communication capacity is a platform team's throughput constraint as much as engineering capacity — staff and budget it explicitly.
insights.quote: Communication is part of the platform. We explain context and impact before implementation and communicate early to avoid surprises.
